name: Painting Numbers
description: You are given $$$n$$$ integers, each integer is from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$, all of them are pairwise distinct. You have to paint them red and blue (each integer should have exactly one color). The cost of painting is the number of pairs $$$(x, y)$$$ such that $$$y \bmod x = 0$$$, $$$y$$$ is red and $$$x$$$ is blue. For each $$$k \in [1, n]$$$, calculate the maximum cost of painting if exactly $$$k$$$ integers should have a red color.
input_specification: The first line contains one integer $$$n$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 10^5$$$).
output_specification: For each $$$k \in [1,n]$$$ print one integer — the maximum cost of painting, if exactly $$$k$$$ integers should be red.
approach_summary: Precompute linear sieve to store minimum prime factor (spf[x]) up to N in O(N). Factorize any number x ≤ N in O(log x) steps.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1488G — Painting Numbers [242. Sieve, Prime Factorization and Divisors]
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Every composite integer $X$ has at least one prime factor $\le \sqrt{X}$. Precomputing the Smallest Prime Factor (SPF) for all numbers up to $M$ via a linear sieve allows any $X \le M$ to be completely prime-factorized in $O(\log X)$ steps.
